summaries.example: Imagine two identical toy blocks. Each block is square and made of plastic. Those features seem to belong to the blocks themselves. But one block might be next to a red ball, while the other is not. Being next to the ball depends on what is around the block, so it is an extrinsic feature.
summaries.summary: The entry explains a common philosophical difference between intrinsic and extrinsic properties. An intrinsic property belongs to something because of the way that thing is. An extrinsic property depends partly on other things or on the wider situation. A person's mass is a familiar example of an intrinsic property, while being an uncle depends on a family connection. The difference sounds simple, but difficult examples show that it may include several different ideas. One idea asks whether a description is only about the thing and its parts. Another asks whether removing the rest of the world would leave the property unchanged. A third asks whether perfect duplicates must share the property. These tests do not always give the same answers. Philosophers therefore study several kinds of intrinsicality rather than assuming there is one easy definition.
key_ideas: Mass, shape, and material are often treated as intrinsic properties.
Being an uncle or being a certain distance from a flower depends on other things, so these are often treated as extrinsic.
Philosophers disagree about some cases, such as whether shape is always intrinsic.
The words intrinsic and extrinsic are used in several related ways, not always in one single way.
These ideas help philosophers think about change, value, minds, knowledge, and what kinds of situations are possible.
summaries.why_it_matters: This distinction helps us ask what really belongs to a thing and what depends on its setting. It can help explain why a person's death seems to change the person who dies, while it changes another person's relationship status in a different way. It also appears in questions about what is valuable in itself, how minds depend on physical features, how knowledge depends on a thinker, and which combinations of properties are possible. Learning the distinction also teaches an important lesson about philosophy: an everyday idea can be useful while still needing careful examination.

important_terms.definition: A feature something has because of what it is like in itself, including its parts and how those parts fit together.
A feature something has partly because of its surroundings or its connections with other things.
A feature or way something is, such as being square, heavy, or being an uncle.
A thing that is exactly alike in the ways being compared, even if it is in a different place or situation.

questions_to_think_about: Is being the tallest person in a room intrinsic or extrinsic? Why?
If two objects are perfect duplicates but placed in different surroundings, which of their properties might differ?
Could something have an extrinsic property in a way that still seems to depend only on itself?
Why might philosophers want to know whether a change is a real change or only a change in what we call something?

summaries.example: Consider a metal object that is 1 metre from a second object. Its mass and internal structure are natural candidates for intrinsic properties. Its being an uncle is clearly extrinsic because it depends on a family relation involving someone outside the object. Distance is more controversial: some philosophers regard spatial relations as intrinsic to the related objects, while others think distance depends on features of the surrounding space. The example shows why apparently simple classifications can depend on deeper metaphysical commitments.
summaries.summary: The entry begins with an intuitive contrast: intrinsic properties belong to an object in virtue of the object itself, whereas extrinsic properties depend on relations or a wider context. Standard examples include mass and internal structure on the intrinsic side, and being an uncle or being a certain distance from another object on the extrinsic side. However, closer examination reveals that several nearby distinctions may be involved. A property may be local because its description concerns an object and its parts, interior because it is a matter of how the object is, or duplication-preserving because duplicates cannot differ with respect to it. These classifications can come apart. For instance, identity properties and properties that everything necessarily has create problems for simple duplication tests. The entry surveys attempts to analyze the distinction using logical resources, fundamental or perfectly natural properties, non-disjunctive properties, contractions of possible worlds, and grounding. Each approach illuminates part of the idea but encounters objections. The discussion therefore treats intrinsicality as a family of related notions, while noting reasons philosophers may most often intend an identity-based form of interiority.
key_ideas: The ordinary contrast between intrinsic and extrinsic properties appears to combine several distinctions: relational versus non-relational, local versus non-local, interior versus exterior, and duplication preservation.

An object can have an extrinsic property in an intrinsic fashion under some tests. For example, a piece of tin has the property of being either made of tin or married in a way that every duplicate also has, even though the property itself mentions a possible relation.
The distinction has applications in ethics, metaphysics, philosophy of mind, epistemology, and theories of possibility.
Different analyses appeal to broadly logical notions, fundamental properties, non-disjunctivity, contractions of worlds, or metaphysical grounding.
Proposed analyses face counterexamples, circularity worries, or dependence on controversial assumptions about properties and possible worlds.
The entry suggests that identity-based interiority may be the dominant notion in philosophical usage, but the reasons are not decisive and no single analysis is established.
summaries.why_it_matters: Intrinsicness is not merely a vocabulary exercise. In ethics, it informs the contrast between value that is good in itself and value that is good as a means. In metaphysics, it bears on real change, persistence through time, and the distinction between objects changing and merely acquiring new relational descriptions. In philosophy of mind and epistemology, claims about mental states or justification sometimes say that they depend only on a thinker’s intrinsic features. The concept also shapes principles about recombining properties into possible worlds. important_terms.definition: A property had in virtue of the way an object itself is, rather than in virtue of how it relates to things outside it.
A property whose possession depends, at least partly, on relations to other things or on a larger context.
The claim that a fact or property is fixed by, or depends on, some specified class of facts or properties, without necessarily being identical to them.
The relation of metaphysical explanation: one fact grounds another when the first helps explain why the second obtains.
A property that does not differ between perfect duplicates, across the relevant possible situations.
A property whose ascription concerns how an object and its parts are, rather than how they relate to wholly separate things.
A proposed fundamental property or relation that helps describe reality without depending on less fundamental descriptions.
A theory that treats an object’s intrinsic properties as those that remain unchanged when the rest of its world is removed as far as possible.

questions_to_think_about: Why does the fact that a property is relational not by itself show that it is extrinsic?
Does a perfect duplicate have to share every property, or only every intrinsic or qualitative property?
Why might the property of being an uncle be a useful test case for theories of intrinsicness?
Can an analysis of intrinsicness avoid presupposing the very idea it is meant to explain?
Which is more convincing: defining intrinsic properties through duplicates, through what a thing is in itself, or through what remains after removing its surroundings?

summaries.example: Suppose two new bicycles are exactly alike in their parts and shape. One is leaning against a wall, and the other is standing alone. Leaning against the wall seems extrinsic because it depends on another object. Being made of metal seems intrinsic. But being the fastest bicycle in the race is also different: it depends on how the bicycle compares with competitors. This helps show that some features belong to a thing, while others depend on its surroundings or comparisons.
summaries.summary: The entry studies the familiar idea that intrinsic properties come from the way a thing is in itself, while extrinsic properties depend on other things or a larger setting. Mass and internal structure are standard candidates for intrinsic properties; being an uncle and being a certain distance from a particular plant are standard extrinsic examples. Yet the intuitive idea becomes complicated. One proposal focuses on whether a statement is entirely about the object and its parts. Another focuses on whether the object has the property simply in virtue of how it is. A third says that perfect duplicates should agree about intrinsic properties. These proposals divide into related notions such as local properties, interior properties, and duplication-preserving properties. They do not always classify cases alike. The entry also distinguishes global claims about which properties are intrinsic from local claims about an object’s having a property intrinsically. It then explains why the distinction matters in ethics, theories of change and persistence, supervenience claims about mind and knowledge, and principles about what combinations of properties are possible. Philosophers have proposed analyses based on logic, fundamental properties, non-disjunctive structure, world-contraction, and grounding, but each faces important challenges.
key_ideas: The basic contrast is between what something is like in itself and what depends on its context.
Clear examples exist on both sides, but many properties are disputed or depend on which test is used.
Being relational is not exactly the same as being extrinsic: a property can compare parts within one object and still seem intrinsic.
Philosophers use several tests, including aboutness, dependence on the object itself, and agreement between duplicates.
The distinction helps with questions about value, real change, persistence, minds, knowledge, and possible worlds.
The entry presents competing analyses rather than declaring that one definition has settled the issue.
summaries.why_it_matters: Thinking about intrinsic and extrinsic properties helps separate a thing’s own features from facts about its relationships. That difference matters when deciding whether a change is genuinely a change in an object or only a new description caused by someone else’s situation. It also matters when philosophers ask whether value belongs to something in itself, whether mental facts depend only on a person’s internal features, or whether two worlds can contain similar objects arranged differently. The topic is valuable because it shows how philosophy tests everyday distinctions: a simple idea can guide many debates, yet still contain several meanings that need to be separated.

important_terms.definition: A feature something has because of how it is on its own, including its parts and their arrangement.
A feature something has because of its surroundings, relationships, or place in a larger situation.
A feature that involves how one thing is connected to another, although not every relational feature is automatically extrinsic.
An object that matches another object in all the relevant intrinsic features, even if the two are in different surroundings.
A property that stays the same between duplicates in the possible situations being considered.
A property described as concerning an object and its parts, rather than its connections to outside objects.
A way of saying that one set of facts fixes another set of facts, even though the two sets are not identical.

questions_to_think_about: Is being the oldest student in a class intrinsic or extrinsic? What makes you classify it that way?
Can a property be relational but still intrinsic? Consider a feature that compares an object’s own parts.
If two perfect duplicates are in different places, must they have all the same properties?
Why might a philosopher distinguish a real change in an object from a change in how the object is described?
What problem would arise if every property that never differs between duplicates were called intrinsic?
